final_answer:
Bottom line (as of April 1, 2026): The husband should file, with the immigration court that entered the August 1, 2025 in absentia order, a motion to reopen to rescind the order for lack of notice under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) / 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii), and he should do it promptly. There is no deadline for a lack-of-notice motion. Filing it automatically stays removal until the IJ rules. Based on EOIR guidance, no EOIR fee applies to a lack-of-notice motion. The fee does apply to an exceptional-circumstances motion, which would also be time-barred here because the 180 days ran in January 2026. Related USCIS steps are separate.

1. The court filing. The motion goes to the Immigration Judge. It must be supported by a sworn declaration from the husband (and ideally the wife) stating that neither of them ever received the NTA or any hearing notice. The declaration should say the Mexican-resident couple never gave USCIS or EOIR the address used, and should attach the I-130/I-485 filing receipts and forms showing the correct address, any AR-11 or change-of-address filings, and the RFE and denial notices showing the same wrong address. It must include a certificate of service on DHS/ICE OPLA. Counsel files an EOIR-28; the husband may also need an EOIR-33 change-of-address form, and he should check the ECAS/automated case information for his A-number. The motion should also request that the in absentia order be rescinded and proceedings reopened, and it should expressly invoke the automatic stay. One motion to rescind is allowed, so it should be thorough. Under Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), he must show he did not receive notice under either INA 239(a)(1) (the NTA) or 239(a)(2) (the notice of hearing) for the hearing he missed. Here the NTA and, presumably, the hearing notice went to the same address the couple never provided, so the facts should support this. Verify from the record (FOIA/ROP) exactly what was mailed where. Rescission is not automatic: the presumption of delivery for regular mail is weaker than for certified mail (Matter of M-R-A-, 24 I&N Dec. 665 (BIA 2008)), but a respondent needs affirmative evidence beyond a bare denial. Adverse authority to watch: search results indicate that on September 3, 2026 the BIA decided Matter of Diji, 30 I&N Dec. 1, which overruled Matter of G-Y-R- and lets DHS rely on the most recent address the person provided, including one given before the NTA issued. That post-dates the April 1, 2026 as-of date and I did not read the opinion. It would not seem to help DHS where, as here, the address was never provided by the respondent, but this point should be checked.

2. EOIR fees. A motion to reopen or reconsider an IJ decision carries an OBBBA fee, set at $1,045 for FY2026 (effective February 1, 2026). Per EOIR guidance and practitioner summaries, that fee does not apply to a motion to reopen an in absentia order under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (lack of notice). So the fee should be $0 for the rescission motion. I could not open the Federal Register or the regulation text directly (the fetch was blocked), so this fee exemption rests on search-result summaries and should be confirmed before filing. If the court rejects the filing for fee reasons, the fallback is to cite the exemption or file a fee waiver request (some OBBBA fees are not waivable). Costs for later steps are separate. If the order is rescinded and proceedings reopened, the husband can then renew his adjustment application before the IJ (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1)); the I-485 fee is $1,440 paid to DHS per the USCIS fee schedule, and a new I-130, if needed, is $675 paper or $625 online. Confirm each against current Form G-1055 before filing, because fee schedules change.

3. Contesting the I-130 and I-485 denials. The I-130 was denied for abandonment (no RFE response). Under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15) such a denial cannot be appealed, but the petitioner may file a motion to reopen under 8 CFR 103.5 (Form I-290B, fee $800 per search summaries). The 30-day deadline has long passed, but 103.5(a)(2) lets USCIS excuse lateness where the delay was reasonable and beyond the filer's control. Non-receipt due to USCIS mailing to an address the couple never gave is the strongest such argument, and USCIS has the discretion to reopen on its own motion. Do not rely on this alone; USCIS's treatment of a motion filed 2+ years late is uncertain. The more reliable route is for the U.S.-citizen wife to file a new I-130 (and, if the order is rescinded, ask the IJ for a continuance under Matter of Hashmi, 24 I&N Dec. 785 (BIA 2009), pending USCIS adjudication; the Hashmi factors include whether the petition is prima facie approvable, whether he is eligible for adjustment, and the DHS position). The I-485 denial followed from the I-130 denial and cannot be appealed. Once the order is rescinded, the IJ has jurisdiction to adjudicate the I-485 de novo, but cannot approve the I-130 himself, which stays with USCIS.

4. Substantive eligibility risks. As the spouse of a U.S. citizen who was inspected and admitted on a B-2, he is an immediate relative and is not barred by overstay (INA 245(c) exceptions), so his I-94 expiry on June 1, 2023 is not itself a bar. But marriage 19 days after entry invites a preconceived-intent / misrepresentation inquiry (State Department 90-day rule, applied by analogy; I did not research it in this run) and the bona fides of the marriage must be shown with strong evidence. An in absentia order's 10-year bar on adjustment under INA 240(b)(7) applies only if notice was properly given, so it should not apply if rescission is granted.

5. Sequence recommendation. (a) File the rescission motion now; (b) concurrently or promptly file a new I-130 and, if desired, an I-290B/late motion; (c) after rescission, file the I-485 with the court, and request a continuance if I-130 is pending. If the motion to rescind is denied, the BIA appeal (EOIR-26, $1,010 FY2026) and a petition for review in the circuit court within 30 days are the next steps. Because ICE may now treat the order as final, he should avoid travel and consult counsel immediately.

claims.text: Rescission motion on lack of notice may be filed with the IJ at any time and stays removal automatically on filing.
He must show non-receipt of notice under 239(a)(1) or (2) for the missed hearing.
No EOIR OBBBA fee applies to a lack-of-notice rescission motion; the general MTR fee is $1,045 (FY2026).
I-130 abandonment denial is not appealable but a motion to reopen may be filed, with late filing excusable.
After rescission, IJ may continue case pending a new/reopened I-130 and adjudicate I-485.
Later BIA authority on address reliance may be adverse but is distinguishable where address was never provided.
Other filing fees are as listed on G-1055.
